title: Master Class | Crushing The Modern Defense | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Let's unpack this. The bishop to g7 is the Modern, and the move I'm interested in — c3 — is definitely not the most popular; most people just develop the knight.
The mainstream choice is the knight to c3, the natural developing move that grabs a share of the center.
But there's another line, one favored by a lot of strong positional players.
Very positional grandmasters like Kamsky and Tiviakov like to play c3 here. The idea is simple: you're building a big broad pawn center and betting it cramps Black for the long haul.
What's the downside of c3? The obvious one is that the queen's knight can no longer develop to c3 — but it's perfectly happy rerouting through d2 instead. Black settles in with d6.
The whole point is to blunt that g7-bishop, to get it biting on a wall of pawns rather than an open diagonal — just a line worth considering against the Modern.
In the actual game c5 was a bad pre-move — Black fired it off expecting the knight to c3.
He was assuming the knight would come to c3, and against that particular move order c5 actually
is a viable line — with the knight already committed to c3, striking with c5 has real bite.

The point is that after d takes c5, the queen to a5 sets up two threats at once: the bishop takes c3 with check, winning the knight, and the queen takes c5, regaining the pawn — Black is doing fine here.
